title: Shoot! The Game
author: ZeonisLow
selftext:
Hey everyone! I'm a CS student, and for the past several weeks I've been making \*\*Shoot!\*\*, a Rock-Paper-Scissors ninja platform fighter. I've been working with Claude (Anthropic's AI) as my main coding partner the whole way. I just finished moving the game from 2D to full 3D in Godot 4, so I wanted to share the trailer and how the AI workflow went.

🎬 \*\*Trailer:\*\* https://youtu.be/oW12C3Yxt3c

\*\*The game\*\*  
Each round starts with a secret call. Both players pick Rock, Paper or Scissors at the same time, then fight as that element's ninja. There are 6 stages, online play (Quick Match, House Rules, King of the Hill), a training mode and 3D instant replays.

\*\*How I used AI\*\*  
\- \*\*Code:\*\* I describe what I want in plain English, Claude writes the GDScript, and I playtest and send feedback. Examples: "let me jump or dodge out of the pogo dive at any point," "make the dust from running vary in size and fade fast."  
\- \*\*Stages and effects:\*\* most of the stage backgrounds and effects are built in code instead of hand-modeled. That includes the starry skies, the reactor, the desert pyramids and the wind on attacks.  
\- \*\*Online play:\*\* the game runs on a deterministic simulation so both players stay in sync. Claude also wrote automated tests that check the two sides stay identical after every change.  
\- \*\*Gameplay clips and the trailer:\*\* recorded straight from the game using Godot's movie writer.  
\- \*\*My part:\*\* the game idea, design decisions, playtesting with friends, and a lot of "that looks off, fix it" feedback.

\*\*What I learned\*\*  
\- Short, specific feedback works best, and screenshots help a lot.  
\- Asking for a short gameplay clip with every update caught a lot of bugs I'd have missed in the code.  
\- Automated tests saved me many times when a new change broke an old one.

Happy to answer questions about the workflow! Feedback on the game is very welcome too.
